description:
Hey, we're Asterisk! We're taking on the “Planet X and SPHEREx” challenge and are looking for a frontend developer. If that sounds like you, or you have some experience in the field, don't hesitate to say hi.

Please also drop a quick note to qxumb6n4j@mozmail.com so we have a way to get back to you. Cheers!
summary: We have developed a website that lets you easily look at the investigate images produced by SPHEREx without having to know the details, or converting them from the FITS files yourself.
details:
It lets you look at the images of a specific area of the sky and see how the objects in that area change over time. Anyone can volunteer, and no astronomy software or FITS knowledge is needed. It’s pretty much the same idea as Backyard Worlds, which has discovered thousands of brown dwarfs with the help of volunteers. (benefit 1)

Normally, if we converted the images on the fly as users requested them, it would take about 3–5 seconds per image, even on a good virtual private server (VPS). That might not sound slow, but imagine if every post in your social media feed took that long to load! (benefit 2)

Our project loads each image in a fraction of a second.

How?

We pre-rendered all of the images.

That must have taken a lot of storage, compute, bandwidth and money!

Not the money. That’s actually one of the coolest parts. It took a lot of bandwidth, storage and compute, but we didn’t pay a dime to pre-render, store or serve the images. (benefit 3)

How?

For storage, we used a Hugging Face Bucket (https://huggingface.co/buckets/maxkuzzmenko/Asterisk). You can get 7 TB of free storage (as of November 15th, 2026) as long as it serves a good purpose, which ours does. The images aren’t only useful for this project, either: they could be reused elsewhere, for example as ML training data for moving-object detection. (benefit 4)

For compute, we used Docker Sandboxes. It’s an unconventional use of the service, but it worked, and we fit comfortably within the free trial credits.

We spun up 4 medium sandboxes in total (4 vCPUs and 8 GB of memory each). The limit was 10 sandboxes and 40 vCPUs running in parallel, but we chose not to max out the bandwidth. We picked medium sandboxes because they have the best balance of processing power to bandwidth, so neither one becomes a bottleneck. Every sandbox gets the same internet speed regardless of its size, so large sandboxes would be limited by bandwidth and small ones by compute.

We also built a small calculator app that works out how many sandboxes we need to hit a specific time goal. It has proven handy, and it helps the project scale. (benefit 5)

Without the free credits, the compute would have cost us around $25. For reference, just uploading the images from AWS to the bucket would have cost more than $400 (at $0.09 per GB, as of November 15th, 2026). That makes our project very budget-efficient. (benefit 6)

As the archive grows, we have to keep converting new FITS files. That’s no longer a big job, so it runs as a mostly idle Docker container on our Hetzner VPS. Our web page runs on Cloudflare Pages.

For our stack, we mainly used Python for the backend and Vite for the frontend. We used Git, hosted on GitLab, for version control. Here's our repo's URL: https://gitlab.com/asterisk935138/asterisk

How were we creative?

  • We turned an estimated hundreds of terabytes of data into something a browser can play like a video.
  • The RA/Dec-to-image lookup uses each image’s own WCS footprint, so it works for any point in the sky instead of being limited to a fixed catalogue, which you can access on https://api.asteriskteam.earth/.
    Example usage: curl "https://api.asteriskteam.earth/search?ra=133.795&dec=-7.245"
  • We apply the same brightness stretch to every image, so the images can be compared directly when blinking.
